DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure (Harbourside Hotel)

## What the proposal says

From 1 June 2026 the hotel would raise its weekend Best Available Rate (BAR) from £145 to £165 and add a two-night minimum on any stay that includes a Saturday. The case rests on four things:
- the hotel is £20–35 below its three competitors;
- last June's £10 rise was followed by higher occupancy;
- guests give it the best value-for-money score in its competitive set;
- a revenue projection of £204,000 a year, described as a floor.

The competitive gap is real. A rise of some size is probably justified. But the projection uses the wrong room count and applies to more rooms than will actually pay the new rate. The price-sensitivity "test" is confounded by the hotel's own seasonal pattern. And the two-night minimum works against the hotel's largest single Saturday segment.

**Arithmetic.** The 2025 average of 79% checks out (950 ÷ 12 = 79.2%). £20 × 124 × 104 × 0.79 = £203,757 is computed correctly, but the inputs are wrong (§2).

## 1. The June 2025 "test" doesn't show low price sensitivity

The proposal says weekend occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July after the £10 increase, and takes this as evidence that guests are "not price sensitive." That inference doesn't hold:

- **July is the hotel's seasonal peak.** Section 2 says so: the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would be expected to rise from June to July regardless of price.
- **Most July bookings were probably made before the rise.** The new rate started in the last week of June. Leisure weekend guests, especially for festival weekends, usually book weeks or months ahead. So much of July's 89% was likely booked at £135.
- **The right comparison is year on year.** Compare weekend occupancy in July 2024 with July 2025, and booking pace for July–September 2025 after the rise. If July 2025 ran below July 2024, the rise may already have cost occupancy.
- **"Reinforced our positioning as a quality option"** is speculation. Nothing in the data supports it.

The value-for-money score doesn't help either:
- **It doesn't measure price sensitivity.** It comes from guests who already chose to stay.
- **It is partly a result of being the cheapest.** Being cheapest is a large part of why value for money scores best. At £165 the hotel will be level with the cheapest competitor, and the score will probably fall.

Together, "everything points the same way" amounts to a confounded comparison and a score that depends on the current low price.

## 2. The £204,000 is not a floor

| Issue | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Room count.** Section 2 says 112 rooms; Section 5 uses 124. | At 112 rooms the same calculation gives **£184,000** |
| **Not every room pays BAR.** The £20 applies only to rooms sold at BAR. Contracted groups, wedding blocks (38% of Saturday bookings), packages and discounted rates won't pay it. | If wedding blocks alone make up roughly a fifth of weekend room-nights, the figure falls toward about **£150,000** |
| **VAT and commission.** UK room rates normally include 20% VAT, and online travel agencies (OTAs) take commission on their bookings. | £20 on the rate is about £16.67 net of VAT, and less again on OTA bookings |
| **Bookings already made.** Stays from 1 June onward already booked at £145 will stay at £145. | Year-one revenue falls further, especially for peak summer |
| **No allowance for lost occupancy.** | See below |

The proposal calls "assumes no occupancy gain" a prudent assumption. That only makes sense if you believe the rise would *increase* occupancy, which §1 doesn't support. The real downside risk is occupancy *loss*.

**Break-even:**
- At £145 and 79% occupancy, revenue per available room is £114.55.
- At £165 the hotel needs **69.4%** occupancy to match it.
- So it can lose about 9.6 points before room revenue falls, before allowing for lost bar, restaurant and breakfast spend from fewer guests.

That is a reasonable cushion, but it should be stated. And the projection should be a range, not a floor.

## 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

Section 4 says wedding guests at Quayside Hall make up **around 38% of Saturday-night bookings**. They book as a block, arrive on Saturday and leave on Sunday. A two-night minimum on every stay that includes a Saturday either:
- turns these guests away,
- forces them to pay for a Friday they won't use, or
- has to be waived for them, which the proposal doesn't say.

"Group rates already contracted will be honoured" covers only weddings that are already booked. Future couples may steer their guests to competitors without a minimum. Wedding demand may also be one reason the hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays.

Two further points:
- **On the other 21 Saturdays, the minimum just turns away one-night guests** with no compensating benefit. Standard revenue-management practice is to apply minimum stays only on dates forecast to sell out.
- **The minimum is a risk, not just upside.** The proposal treats it as unquantified extra revenue, but it could lose Saturday nights. Its effect should be estimated in both directions, or the minimum limited to peak, non-wedding dates with wedding blocks exempt.

## 4. Monitoring

- **The trigger looks backward.** "More than five points below 2025 for any month" can only be checked once a month is over. By then the following months are largely booked. The weekly booking-pace review is the right tool, so the trigger should be written in terms of pace against the same weeks last year.
- **The comparison year is distorted.** The 2025 June–July baseline itself includes the previous rate change.
- **Track revenue per available room, not just occupancy.** A five-point drop in occupancy can be acceptable at the higher rate, given the break-even above, so occupancy alone could trigger a review when none is needed.

## 5. Smaller points

- "Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023" is stated without any data.
- A £20 rise is 14%, almost twice the size of last June's £10 (7%) rise. Even if last year's rise had shown low sensitivity, that wouldn't carry over automatically to a rise twice as large.
- At £165 the hotel will match the cheapest competitor, not stay below it. "Brings our pricing into line" is accurate. "Priced well below our competitive set" (Section 7) won't be once the change takes effect.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the room count to 112 and restate revenue for BAR room-nights only, net of VAT and commission, allowing for bookings already on the books. Give a range rather than a floor.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with year-on-year occupancy and booking-pace data for 2024 and 2025. Remove the claim that guests are not price sensitive.
3. Consider a staged rise, for example £155 now and a review in the autumn, or testing £165 on peak dates first.
4. Restrict the two-night minimum to dates forecast to sell out, exempt wedding and group blocks, and estimate its effect in both directions.
5. Base the monitoring trigger on forward booking pace and revenue per available room.

The underlying case, that the hotel is underpriced against comparable hotels, is reasonable. The evidence that guests won't react, the claim that £204,000 is a floor, and the blanket two-night minimum are not well supported.
